blocks.text: Washington · Digital asset policy
Democrats’ wins reshape the next Congress. They do not turn a stalled crypto market-structure bill into a lame-duck certainty.
By Jack Smack · November 4, 2026
Editorial illustration. The calendar is the story: the outgoing Congress retains the gavel during the lame duck; the incoming Congress inherits the next attempt.
Election night changed the political map. It did not change the vote that stopped the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act in the Senate.

That distinction is easy to lose in the rush to interpret a new majority. The Associated Press called enough races on November 3 to say Democrats had won control of both chambers. It also called Ohio for Sherrod Brown over Republican Jon Husted. But these were election calls, not final state certifications: Ohio’s election office said its posted results were unofficial while canvassing and certification remained ahead.

My read is that the result makes a quick, clean revival of CLARITY less likely, not more. The bill’s immediate fate still rests with the Congress elected in 2024, which retains control until the next Congress convenes in January. Democrats can shape that next Congress’s agenda and committee leadership. They cannot retroactively make the current Senate’s procedural failure disappear.

H.R. 3633, the House-passed Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, moved through the Senate Banking Committee in a substantially revised form. In May, the committee advanced a substitute after bipartisan negotiations. That was meaningful progress, but a committee vote is not a Senate floor coalition.

On September 15, the Senate failed to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed. The official floor record lists the vote as 49–50. Cloture is the procedural step that would have allowed the chamber to move toward debate; failing there meant the bill never reached the floor debate and passage stage. The question is no longer simply whether lawmakers agree that digital-asset rules need clarification. It is whether they can agree on the bill’s actual allocation of authority and protections.
Committee support showed a negotiating coalition. The failed floor vote showed that it was not yet a governing coalition.
The difference between those two things is the difference between a bill that has momentum and one that has a path to enactment.

The outgoing majority still sets the agenda during the post-election session. That creates a theoretical opening for another attempt. Yet no official floor notice or committee schedule I reviewed listed a CLARITY vote for the lame duck. A published return calendar is not a bill-specific commitment.

Congress also faces end-of-year work that competes for scarce floor time. The Senate’s tentative 2026 calendar identifies December 18 as a target adjournment date. That is a planning marker, not a promise that lawmakers will finish on that date—or that they will spend the remaining time on crypto legislation.

There is a further political complication. If the outgoing majority tries to push the bill through after voters have selected a new majority, incoming lawmakers may have little incentive to bless a text they did not shape. That is an inference about legislative incentives, not a public commitment by either party. The election does not prove that a lame-duck deal is impossible; it makes the deal’s politics harder to read.

When the new Congress organizes in January 2027, control of both chambers is expected to shift to Democrats. That should change which party chooses committee chairs in Senate Banking, Senate Agriculture, House Financial Services, and House Agriculture, subject to the chambers’ organization and committee assignments.

The specific incoming chairs and ranking members were not established by election-night results. Nor does party control by itself tell us what any committee will do with crypto policy. Members’ votes and statements on stablecoin yield, decentralized finance, customer safeguards, and the SEC–CFTC boundary are more informative than a simple partisan label. The evidence assembled here does not support a complete member-by-member profile of the new committees.

Text is likely to be part of the negotiation. The Senate committee advanced a substitute to the House-passed bill, so the chambers were already working from different versions. If lawmakers restart the effort in 2027, they may revisit how digital commodities are defined, which activities receive special treatment, what obligations apply to DeFi developers and intermediaries, and how enforcement authority is divided between the SEC and CFTC. Those are pressure points, not predictions of specific amendments.

I assign a 5–15% chance to lame-duck passage, a 55–70% chance that the effort slips into 2027 with revised text, and a 20–35% chance that it stalls without near-term enactment. These are editorial probability ranges, not outputs from a statistical model. They are conditional on the evidence available on November 4, 2026, and should move if leadership schedules floor action or sponsors publish a negotiated agreement.

The ranges are deliberately broad because the key evidence is missing: a published lame-duck schedule, a new cross-party agreement, and a confirmed list of incoming committee leaders. Without those, precision would be theatre.

A formal Senate notice scheduling the bill would raise the lame-duck scenario. So would sponsor statements backed by actual vote commitments and a House plan to accept the Senate text. Conversely, explicit leadership opposition, a crowded end-of-year schedule, or a decision to defer substantive work to the next Congress would push the 2027 path higher.

For the 2027 scenario, the decisive test is not whether new committee chairs use favorable language about innovation or consumer protection. It is whether they publish text, hold hearings or markups, and build a coalition that can survive a floor vote. Until then, committee control is an opportunity to set priorities—not evidence that a particular crypto rulebook is coming.

Democratic control of the next Congress will reshape oversight and agenda-setting. It may also make the industry negotiate over a different balance of market access, investor protection, and agency authority. That is a material political shift for a sector that has treated comprehensive market-structure legislation as a defining federal policy goal.

But the immediate legislative math remains stubborn. The September cloture vote failed; the lame-duck calendar is limited; and the incoming majority has not yet shown what text it would support. The election changed who gets to write the next chapter. It did not write the chapter for them.

bitcoin-open-interest-filter-test.text: Skip to article Crypto ResearchIndependent market analysis / Derivatives Market structure / InvestigationBitcoin’s Open-Interest Filter Failed Its Simplest TestA timestamp correction rescued a plausible derivatives signal from look-ahead bias. It did not show that open interest improves on price momentum.November 4, 2026 · Historical research, not a live market signal Conceptual editorial artwork. The two lines do not represent recorded market prices or open interest. A market signal can look convincing for two very different reasons. It can contain information that prices have not yet absorbed. Or it can appear to work because the test quietly gives it information from the future. Bitcoin’s open-interest story sits uncomfortably close to that boundary. The familiar interpretation is seductive: when Bitcoin rises and futures open interest rises with it, new leveraged positions may be reinforcing the move. When open interest falls, perhaps the rally is merely traders closing shorts. That language gives us a tidy narrative about conviction, positioning and the quality of a trend. But a narrative is not a tradeable edge. What matters is whether the extra variable improves a decision relative to a rule that just watches price—and whether the data were genuinely available when that decision would have been made. In the historical OKX BTC-USDT perpetual dataset examined here, open interest did not clear that bar. An initially troubling timestamp mismatch was substantially reconciled. A modestly profitable hypothetical price-plus-OI strategy survived that correction. Yet a simpler price-momentum strategy still earned higher modeled returns in both available comparison periods. The one-hour problem hiding inside the data Open interest counts outstanding derivatives contracts. It is not a direct measure of bullishness: every contract has a long and a short. The interpretation of rising OI depends on who is initiating risk, the direction of price, funding conditions and the structure of the market. It also depends, less romantically, on which clock the database uses. The original daily and hourly observations for the same instrument initially appeared irreconcilable. At matching printed timestamps, BTC-denominated daily OI differed from hourly OI by an average of about 754 BTC. The daily USD-denominated OI values also differed from BTC OI multiplied by the contemporaneous mark by as much as 6.69%. These were warnings, not evidence of manipulation or a market event. The revised historical panel supplied a more defensible explanation for the first mismatch. Its hourly OI records distinguish an aggregation bar's printed timestamp from an inferred value time one hour later. Once completed daily OI values were compared to hourly OI on that basis, 58 of 59 comparable daily observations matched exactly; the remaining observation was nearly identical, with a maximum relative difference of roughly 0.0000416%. The corrected hourly BTC OI values also reproduced the earlier hourly series across all 1,439 completed records. That reconciliation is substantial, but it has a boundary. It demonstrates agreement within the supplied dataset under a particular time convention. It does not independently prove the provider’s publication latency, and it does not explain every currency- or contract-denominated discrepancy. The smaller gap between reported BTC OI and contracts multiplied by the stated 0.01 BTC multiplier reached about 3.14 BTC. If the timestamp is wrong, the strategy may be betting with tomorrow’s information while claiming to predict tomorrow. This changes how the earlier daily test should be read. The day-level result cannot be treated as a clean, point-in-time predictive experiment once the OI value-time ambiguity is acknowledged. The hourly comparison is more defensible because it deliberately waits: the price candle and corresponding OI interval must finish, and the modeled entry comes at the next hour’s open. The filter earned money on paper. That was not the point. The hourly setup used 1,440 consecutive price observations, 1,439 completed OI observations and 280 funding settlements, with a 24-hour holding period. The rule was deliberately simple: consider a long after both the preceding one-hour price change and the corresponding BTC-denominated OI change are positive. Entries were restricted to nonoverlapping daily opportunities, with a further hour allowed between signal observation and entry. Recorded settlement funding was included; the assumed trading friction was nine basis points per round trip. Over 40 eligible development opportunities from September 6 through October 15, 2026, the price-plus-OI rule generated ten entries and a compounded hypothetical net return of +6.52%. Over 19 later opportunities from October 16 through November 3, it generated five entries and returned +1.19%. On their own, those positive numbers might seem to vindicate the OI thesis. Then comes the necessary comparison: what if the same rule ignored open interest and used price direction alone? What the extra OI filter actually addedOKX BTC-USDT-SWAP; compounded hypothetical strategy returns, unleveraged; recorded funding included and assumed 9 bps round-trip costs deducted. Periods are historical, not forecasts.StrategyDevelopmentSep 6–Oct 15Later periodOct 16–Nov 3Price ↑ and OI ↑+6.52%+1.19%Price momentum only+9.31%+1.78%Daily long, repeated entry−1.15%−7.80%Cash0.00%0.00%The development segment has 40 eligible opportunities; the later segment has 19. Signals triggered 10/5 times for price + OI and 21/11 times for price alone. The later segment was already examined during the wider research process and is not an untouched out-of-sample holdout. Different trading frequencies imply different cost burdens; the repeated daily-long strategy is not continuous buy-and-hold. Source: supplied OKX research datasets and their accompanying reproducible numerical validation, frozen November 4, 2026. The momentum-only baseline came out ahead in both segments: by roughly 2.79 percentage points in development and 0.60 points later. In these windows, filtering for rising OI reduced exposure, but it did not improve the modeled compounded return compared with simply following positive price momentum. Hypothetical net performance: OI filter versus price momentumThe development price-plus-OI strategy returned 6.52 percent versus 9.31 percent for price-only momentum. In the later diagnostic period, the respective returns were 1.19 percent and 1.78 percent. The bars share a zero baseline and a 0 to 10 percent scale.Net return after funding and assumed 9 bps costHistorical, compounded; shared 0–10% scaleDevelopmentLater period02.557.510%6.52%9.31%1.19%1.78%Price + OIPrice momentumBoth segments favor the simpler price-only rule on modeled return. The two groups are not independent evidence of forward predictive performance. Underlying values and assumptions are provided in the table above. The distinction is central. There is a coherent story for why open interest could help: a directional price move accompanied by expanding leverage might carry information about the market’s willingness to add risk. But there is also a coherent opposing story. Crowded leverage may be fragile, the sign of open interest says nothing about who is right, and the filter may discard profitable price moves for no compensating benefit. The comparison in this dataset favors the simpler explanation, while remaining too small to settle the general question. Why costs and funding complicate the answer The backtest incorporated 8-hour funding settlements instead of treating funding as a single arbitrary daily adjustment. For the price-plus-OI rule, the total modeled return was +7.48% in development before trading fees and slippage and +1.64% in the later period. Deducting nine basis points per round trip reduced those figures to +6.52% and +1.19%; raising assumed costs to 20 basis points reduced them again to +5.36% and +0.63%. How fragile are the returns to trading friction?Price ↑ / OI ↑ rule only. Compounded hypothetical return with recorded funding; 0, 9 or 20 basis points of total assumed round-trip costs.Round-trip costDevelopmentLater period0 bps+7.48%+1.64%9 bps+6.52%+1.19%20 bps+5.36%+0.63%Costs are scenarios, not measured fills. Funding is based on recorded historical settlement rates. The calculation does not establish realized spread, queue position, market impact, adverse selection, liquidation costs or the effect of leverage. It is tempting to regard positive results at 20 basis points as proof of robustness. I would not. These are modeled entries and exits at reference prices, not evidence that a trader could consistently obtain those prices at the intended size. And the more frequently a baseline trades, the more often a flat per-trade cost penalizes it. That makes execution design part of the comparison, not a footnote. There is a further statistical problem. A profitable segment does not tell us whether the difference from a simpler baseline is meaningful when the OI rule makes only ten trades in one period and five in another. No reliable claim of incremental statistical significance follows from counts that small. Nor can the later segment be renamed a pristine holdout simply because it appears after the first segment on a chart: it was already exposed to previous research decisions. The harder interpretation of open interest Open interest remains useful market context. It can describe the extent of outstanding risk and, alongside funding, liquidation activity and order-book depth, help distinguish superficially similar price moves. The error is to turn that contextual value into an untested claim of predictive power. It matters, too, that the instrument here is a single venue’s BTC-USDT perpetual swap, not the whole Bitcoin market. Exchange-specific position growth can reflect hedging, basis trades or venue shifts as readily as directional speculation. Without independently establishing the identity, timestamp and aggregation of each observation, broad claims about “Bitcoin leverage” become fragile. The strongest counterargument to the negative result is that the rule is too crude. A binary increase in price and OI ignores the magnitude of the changes, volatility regime, spot flows, the level of funding, basis and where leverage is concentrated. A more carefully specified model might extract something useful. But greater complexity also opens the door to overfitting; the burden of proof rises, not falls. What would change my assessment is straightforward: a prespecified signal tested on genuinely new observations collected after the November 4, 2026 research freeze; timestamped OI values whose availability is independently confirmed; comparable execution and funding assumptions for every strategy; and an improvement over price momentum that survives realistic costs, alternative regimes and uncertainty estimates. No such forward observations are contained in the supplied files. A useful failure The most instructive result is not that a BTC derivatives strategy made 6.52% in one modeled window. It is that the apparent sophistication of the extra variable did not translate into a better comparison. Once timing was taken seriously and a plain momentum benchmark was put beside the filtered rule, the story became less exciting—and more informative. That is where I land: open interest can deepen a market explanation without deserving a place in the trading decision. Until it proves otherwise against a simpler alternative on genuinely unseen data, its proper role is a question to investigate, not an answer to trade. Data, definitions and limitationsThe historical research covers OKX BTC-USDT-SWAP hourly prices from September 5 through November 4, 2026, the reconciled hourly open-interest series, and 280 recorded 8-hour funding settlements from August 3 through November 4, 2026. Results are as of the November 4, 2026 data freeze; they are not live market conditions. The test uses BTC-denominated OI changes and historical reference-price execution, rather than actual trade fills.The development window contains 40 eligible daily entry opportunities, September 6–October 15; the later diagnostic window contains 19, October 16–November 3. Signals require positive changes in both one-hour price and OI; modeled entry is one hour after the information becomes available, with a fixed 24-hour hold. Positive funding means a long position pays. Long-only returns use unleveraged compounding, with cash when the rule is inactive. No uncertainty interval or significance claim is asserted.Source attribution: supplied historical research datasets identified as originating from OKX public market data, plus the associated numerical validation. The reporting conventions can be compared with the official OKX API documentation; this general documentation link is not proof of the precise hourly value-time semantics. Exact data-vintage and response-retrieval timing were not independently certified. The earlier daily-frequency result is excluded from affirmative evidence because of unresolved point-in-time timing.Illustration and embedded bar chart serve different purposes: the hero is conceptual art; the comparison chart uses the exact rounded hypothetical returns reported in the research. This article is an analytical examination of historical data, not a recommendation or an assurance of strategy performance. Crypto Research · Historical market structure analysis · November 4, 2026

In these windows, filtering for rising OI reduced exposure, but it did not improve the modeled compounded return compared with simply following positive price momentum.

Both segments favor the simpler price-only rule on modeled return. The two groups are not independent evidence of forward predictive performance. Underlying values and assumptions are provided in the table above.

The distinction is central. There is a coherent story for why open interest could help: a directional price move accompanied by expanding leverage might carry information about the market’s willingness to add risk. But there is also a coherent opposing story. Crowded leverage may be fragile, the sign of open interest says nothing about who is right, and the filter may discard profitable price moves for no compensating benefit. The comparison in this dataset favors the simpler explanation, while remaining too small to settle the general question.

The backtest incorporated 8-hour funding settlements instead of treating funding as a single arbitrary daily adjustment. For the price-plus-OI rule, the total modeled return was +7.48% in development before trading fees and slippage and +1.64% in the later period. Deducting nine basis points per round trip reduced those figures to +6.52% and +1.19%; raising assumed costs to 20 basis points reduced them again to +5.36% and +0.63%.
Price ↑ / OI ↑ rule only. Compounded hypothetical return with recorded funding; 0, 9 or 20 basis points of total assumed round-trip costs.

Costs are scenarios, not measured fills. Funding is based on recorded historical settlement rates. The calculation does not establish realized spread, queue position, market impact, adverse selection, liquidation costs or the effect of leverage.

It is tempting to regard positive results at 20 basis points as proof of robustness. I would not. These are modeled entries and exits at reference prices, not evidence that a trader could consistently obtain those prices at the intended size. And the more frequently a baseline trades, the more often a flat per-trade cost penalizes it. That makes execution design part of the comparison, not a footnote.

There is a further statistical problem. A profitable segment does not tell us whether the difference from a simpler baseline is meaningful when the OI rule makes only ten trades in one period and five in another. No reliable claim of incremental statistical significance follows from counts that small. Nor can the later segment be renamed a pristine holdout simply because it appears after the first segment on a chart: it was already exposed to previous research decisions.

Open interest remains useful market context. It can describe the extent of outstanding risk and, alongside funding, liquidation activity and order-book depth, help distinguish superficially similar price moves. The error is to turn that contextual value into an untested claim of predictive power.

It matters, too, that the instrument here is a single venue’s BTC-USDT perpetual swap, not the whole Bitcoin market. Exchange-specific position growth can reflect hedging, basis trades or venue shifts as readily as directional speculation. Without independently establishing the identity, timestamp and aggregation of each observation, broad claims about “Bitcoin leverage” become fragile.

The strongest counterargument to the negative result is that the rule is too crude. A binary increase in price and OI ignores the magnitude of the changes, volatility regime, spot flows, the level of funding, basis and where leverage is concentrated. A more carefully specified model might extract something useful. But greater complexity also opens the door to overfitting; the burden of proof rises, not falls.

What would change my assessment is straightforward: a prespecified signal tested on genuinely new observations collected after the November 4, 2026 research freeze; timestamped OI values whose availability is independently confirmed; comparable execution and funding assumptions for every strategy; and an improvement over price momentum that survives realistic costs, alternative regimes and uncertainty estimates. No such forward observations are contained in the supplied files.

The most instructive result is not that a BTC derivatives strategy made 6.52% in one modeled window. It is that the apparent sophistication of the extra variable did not translate into a better comparison. Once timing was taken seriously and a plain momentum benchmark was put beside the filtered rule, the story became less exciting—and more informative.

That is where I land: open interest can deepen a market explanation without deserving a place in the trading decision. Until it proves otherwise against a simpler alternative on genuinely unseen data, its proper role is a question to investigate, not an answer to trade.

The historical research covers OKX BTC-USDT-SWAP hourly prices from September 5 through November 4, 2026, the reconciled hourly open-interest series, and 280 recorded 8-hour funding settlements from August 3 through November 4, 2026. Results are as of the November 4, 2026 data freeze; they are not live market conditions. The test uses BTC-denominated OI changes and historical reference-price execution, rather than actual trade fills.

The development window contains 40 eligible daily entry opportunities, September 6–October 15; the later diagnostic window contains 19, October 16–November 3. Signals require positive changes in both one-hour price and OI; modeled entry is one hour after the information becomes available, with a fixed 24-hour hold. Positive funding means a long position pays. Long-only returns use unleveraged compounding, with cash when the rule is inactive. No uncertainty interval or significance claim is asserted.

Source attribution: supplied historical research datasets identified as originating from OKX public market data, plus the associated numerical validation. The reporting conventions can be compared with the official OKX API documentation; this general documentation link is not proof of the precise hourly value-time semantics. Exact data-vintage and response-retrieval timing were not independently certified. The earlier daily-frequency result is excluded from affirmative evidence because of unresolved point-in-time timing.

Illustration and embedded bar chart serve different purposes: the hero is conceptual art; the comparison chart uses the exact rounded hypothetical returns reported in the research. This article is an analytical examination of historical data, not a recommendation or an assurance of strategy performance.

binance-four-hour-wallet-takeover.text: INDEPENDENT MARKET NOTES / RESEARCH & INVESTIGATIONSBlockchain forensics · Security & custodyBinance's Four-Hour Wallet Takeover: 50 Authorizations, One Malicious Delegation, and a Delayed RevocationThe chain records the takeover and its end to the second. It cannot tell us why the emergency response took nearly four hours.November 4, 2026 · Historical transaction reconstruction · Ethereum mainnetEditorial illustration based on verified transaction timestamps; not a screenshot of blockchain data.The revealing number in the Binance wallet compromise is not the multibillion-dollar loss. It is one: one valid authorization hidden among 50 submitted signatures, sufficient to hand execution authority over an exchange hot wallet to a different contract. That authority remained in place for almost four hours before a successful on-chain revocation. There are two distinct stories here. One is visible on Ethereum, where transactions have block numbers, timestamps and authorization records. The other happened inside Binance: the detection alerts, decisions, signing controls and emergency procedures. The first story is unusually precise. The second remains largely dependent on Binance's account. Confusing the two would make this investigation sound more certain than the evidence allows. My central conclusion is narrower—and more consequential—than saying a particular wallet technology failed. Stopping ordinary withdrawals is not the same as extinguishing delegated on-chain authority. The Binance 14 incident illustrates that separation with remarkable clarity. The transaction that changed the wallet's authority At 20:20:59 UTC on October 29, 2026, an Ethereum type-4 transaction in block 26,300,753 submitted 50 EIP-7702 authorizations for the address commonly labeled Binance 14: 0x28C6c06298d514Db089934071355E5743bf21d60. Public address metadata identifies the wallet as a Binance hot wallet; such labels are third-party attribution, not consensus-level proof of ownership. The authorizations targeted the same delegation address, 0x63e842B054Bd624a465454D533C33F573e9c6fAe. Their nonces formed a consecutive range from 18,914,775 to 18,914,824. Forty-nine were rejected with an invalid_nonce status. One—nonce 18,914,809—was accepted. That distinction matters. Fifty entries did not mean 50 successful delegations. The batch offered many candidate nonces against a busy account; only one had to match. The transaction record demonstrates the result. It does not establish precisely how the signatures were obtained. One valid authorization among 50Fifty equal-width cells represent the consecutive authorization nonces 18914775 through 18914824. One cell at nonce 18914809 is highlighted as accepted; the remaining 49 are invalid.50 submitted authorizations49 invalid nonces1 accepted: 18,914,809Historical transaction authorization results · Ethereum block 26,300,753Authorization outcomes in the recorded transaction. Each bar represents one authorization entry, not a separate transaction. Source: Ethereum transaction record. Three minutes later, assets began moving At 20:24:23 UTC, another transaction in block 26,300,770 called Binance 14 from the same operator address that submitted the delegation: 0x7C8601d4645b93cea45F71e118A729332e6B5CA0. The transaction's token-transfer records include approximately 1.6154 billion USDT moving from Binance 14 to 0x5227f603C1eE34CE3c06eFe6477003BDfCCB2f8c. Records also identify transfers of RLUSD, WBETH, XAUT and UNI to that recipient. These are historical token quantities, not estimates of their current dollar value. The complete multichain loss and the full inventory of this sweep are not established by this subset of records. For readers accustomed to ordinary exchange withdrawals, this is the essential technical turn. The operator was not merely clicking a withdrawal button. A delegated execution path could invoke wallet behavior on-chain. Disabling a customer-facing withdrawal service does not automatically revoke an authorization that Ethereum itself still recognizes. What EIP-7702 does—and does not explain EIP-7702 allows an externally owned Ethereum account to authorize execution through contract code. The authorization carries an account identity, a chain identifier, a nonce and a target address. A later authorization targeting the zero address can clear the delegation. That is a designed capability, not proof of a protocol vulnerability. It can support useful wallet behavior; it also means that whoever obtains a valid authorization may alter how the account executes. The relevant security question is who could authorize the change, which policies constrained it, and how quickly the owner could undo it. Binance's preliminary report describes a longer intrusion beginning with compromised developer devices, fraudulent recruitment activity, stolen credentials and access to wallet-signing infrastructure. It says an internal AI tool was used during lateral movement. Those details are material, but they are company-reported incident findings, not conclusions independently recoverable from Ethereum transaction history. The final drain and the revocation The late-stage evidence is particularly stark. At 23:55:47 UTC, records show approximately 2,961.99 ETH arriving at Binance 14. At 23:56:47 UTC, a successful transaction in block 26,301,828 produced an internal transfer of 2,961.910820938285 ETH out of that wallet. The incoming transfer's operational purpose is not established. It would be unjustified to claim Binance knowingly routed deposits into a compromised address. What the sequence does show is that assets were still leaving the delegated wallet shortly before the final revocation. At 00:10:35 UTC on October 30, Binance 14 sent a successful type-4 transaction in block 26,301,896 to itself. Its authorization list specified the zero address as the delegation target. The transaction nonce was 18,914,903; the authorization nonce was 18,914,904. That next-nonce relationship is consistent with EIP-7702's rules. The successful zero-address authorization confirms the reported revocation mechanism at transaction level. It does not, without a separate historical code-state comparison, independently establish every byte of the account's before-and-after code state. Verified Ethereum transaction milestones, October 29–30, 2026 (UTC)EventTimestampBlockEvidenceDelegation acceptedOct 29, 20:20:5926,300,753One valid authorization among 50Initial token sweepOct 29, 20:24:2326,300,770Successful token transfersLate ETH outflowOct 29, 23:56:4726,301,8282,961.910820938285 ETH internal transferZero-address revocationOct 30, 00:10:3526,301,896Successful EIP-7702 authorization Ethereum delegation windowThe delegation was accepted October 29 at 20:20:59 UTC and revoked October 30 at 00:10:35 UTC, an elapsed 3 hours 49 minutes 36 seconds. The initial sweep occurred at 20:24:23 and the late ETH outflow at 23:56:47.3 hours, 49 minutes, 36 secondsDelegatedRevoked20:20:5900:10:35Initial sweep: 20:24:23Late ETH outflow: 23:56:47Historical Ethereum events, plotted along a linear elapsed-time axis; intermediate labels are simplified for legibility. Sources: linked transaction records. Four hours of delegated authority is not four hours after detection From the accepted delegation at 20:20:59 UTC to the successful revocation at 00:10:35 UTC, 3 hours, 49 minutes and 36 seconds elapsed. That is a measured blockchain interval. It should not be renamed an incident-response delay after detection. Binance says it detected unusual transfers, suspended withdrawals and worked to revoke the malicious permission. But the exact alert timestamp, the point at which responders understood the delegation mechanism, and the chronology of attempted countermeasures are not established by the transaction records. The difference is not semantic. Without those times, nobody outside the incident team can calculate a reliable detection-to-revocation interval. Was this a failure of emergency readiness? There is a tempting verdict: the exchange lacked a ready-to-run revocation procedure. Binance's own description says its multi-party computation signing arrangement complicated the response and that a specialized procedure was developed. That makes emergency readiness a serious line of inquiry. It does not settle the case. One possibility is that no tested emergency path existed. Another is that a path existed but could not safely satisfy signing policies, nonce requirements or compromised-system isolation under the circumstances. A third is that responders deliberately sequenced containment and validation before submitting a revocation. These explanations carry different implications for governance and engineering quality. The 50-authorization batch demonstrates why nonce management matters: the attacker prepared a range of candidate nonces against a busy wallet. But it does not establish that nonce contention caused the nearly four-hour interval. Internal signing logs, runbooks, escalation records and rejected revocation attempts would be needed to determine that. Nor would it be sound to declare multi-party computation inherently insecure. MPC may reduce the risk of a single stolen key. Its usefulness in a crisis depends on whether the organization can exercise the necessary authority quickly, safely and under attack. A custody architecture can be resistant to theft yet operationally difficult to recover. Attribution is not the same as transaction proof The FBI attributed the operation to North Korea-linked TraderTraitor activity and published associated addresses. That is a significant government finding. The public advisory does not disclose all the intelligence behind the attribution, so the chain records alone should not be presented as proof of an operator's nationality or organizational identity. There is also a distinction between the initial operator address, the wallet whose authority was delegated, the first token recipient and downstream consolidation addresses. The initial operator and recipient are visible in the transaction records cited here. A complete reconciliation of all FBI-listed addresses and the subsequent laundering graph remains outside the demonstrated transaction path. That gap matters when estimating how much was recovered, frozen or still movable. What the breach says about custody Binance reported an overall incident impact of approximately $6.34 billion and about $2.85 billion frozen or intercepted as of its November 3 account. Those are company estimates, not a fully reconciled independent asset-and-liability ledger. Freezing assets is not equivalent to returning them to customers, and replenishing a balance does not by itself establish how the replacement was funded. For the broader financial and governance consequences, see Crypto’s November Stress Test. The lesson I draw from the Ethereum evidence is about control boundaries. A customer withdrawal switch, a signing policy, an on-chain authorization and an emergency revocation are different systems. In calm conditions, they may appear to act as one. During an intrusion, the gaps between them become the attack surface. A stronger custody standard would therefore ask not only whether an attacker can steal a signing credential, but whether an exchange can demonstrate a rehearsed, independently authorized path to extinguish compromised execution authority. That is a question for exchange operators, auditors and customers alike. It is not a claim that every wallet using EIP-7702 faces the same risk. The unanswered question is the one that matters most The public blockchain tells us when authority changed, which authorization succeeded, what moved in the sampled transactions and when the zero-address revocation executed. It does not tell us what Binance's responders knew at each minute, what they tried, or which constraints were unavoidable. That is where the next credible investigation belongs: a documented comparison between the first alert, the first recognition of malicious delegation, the first feasible revocation attempt and the final successful transaction. Such evidence could strengthen the emergency-readiness criticism—or materially weaken it. For now, the strongest conclusion is also the most useful one. A wallet can be administratively frozen while its delegated on-chain authority remains active. Binance 14's recorded history makes that risk concrete. The unresolved issue is not whether the delegation lasted nearly four hours. It is why terminating it took that long—and whether the next exchange facing the same problem will be ready sooner. The chain records cited here support the specific authorization and transfer observations, not a complete forensic accounting of the multichain incident. That distinction matters. Fifty entries did not mean 50 successful delegations. The batch offered many candidate nonces against a busy account; only one had to match. The transaction record demonstrates the result. It does not establish precisely how the signatures were obtained.

The difference is not semantic. Without those times, nobody outside the incident team can calculate a reliable detection-to-revocation interval.

Binance's own description says its multi-party computation signing arrangement complicated the response and that a specialized procedure was developed. That makes emergency readiness a serious line of inquiry. It does not settle the case.

One possibility is that no tested emergency path existed. Another is that a path existed but could not safely satisfy signing policies, nonce requirements or compromised-system isolation under the circumstances. A third is that responders deliberately sequenced containment and validation before submitting a revocation. These explanations carry different implications for governance and engineering quality.

The lesson I draw from the Ethereum evidence is about control boundaries. A customer withdrawal switch, a signing policy, an on-chain authorization and an emergency revocation are different systems. That is where the next credible investigation belongs: a documented comparison between the first alert, the first recognition of malicious delegation, the first feasible revocation attempt and the final successful transaction. For now, the strongest conclusion is also the most useful one. A wallet can be administratively frozen while its delegated on-chain authority remains active. crypto-chokepoints-november-2026.text: Independent Market NotesResearch / November 2026Investigations · Market structureCrypto’s November Stress Test: Liquidity, Custody and the Limits of ControlFrom exchange thefts and frozen stablecoins to election-driven legislation and a sanctioned Moscow trading venue, the same question keeps resurfacing: who can actually move the money?November 4, 2026 · Historical research snapshotEditorial illustration; not a depiction of actual market data or an identified incident.The most revealing number in crypto this week is not a token price. It is the gap between an asset that exists on a ledger and an asset that can actually be moved, redeemed or recovered. That gap runs through the reported Binance theft, a separate European financial-institution attack, an uneven DeFi rebound, and Moscow Exchange’s proposed crypto market. It also helps explain why election headlines and ETF flows should not be mistaken for settled outcomes. My reading of the available evidence is that crypto’s most important November story is a contest over control. Blockchains can make transfers visible, but they cannot by themselves establish who owns an exchange account, compel a custodian to release funds, guarantee stablecoin redemption or turn a legislative proposal into law. The practical market sits between the ledger and the institutions that make it usable. Theft accounting is not the same as recovered money Binance reported approximately $6.34 billion in assets impacted by an October 29, 2026 attack, describing roughly $2.85 billion as frozen or intercepted in its November 3 account. Subtracting those figures produces about $3.49 billion not confirmed secured. That residual is not an audited measure of proceeds successfully cashed out, and it is not necessarily a current-price valuation of attacker holdings. Separate tracing described large balances remaining identifiable in attacker-controlled wallets. A reported Bitquery snapshot at 09:10 UTC on November 3 valued tracked holdings at about $3 billion. That observation supports the possibility of future sell pressure, but a wallet balance is not a sell order. It is equally important that an issuer freeze is not the same as a legal recovery, and a customer reimbursement is not proof the original tokens have been returned. Different measures of the Binance incident; figures are approximate and not additive.MeasureReported amountWhat it establishesInitial impacted value$6.34BTheft-time incident estimateFrozen or intercepted$2.85BReported restrictions or interception, not completed restitutionUnconfirmed secured~$3.49BArithmetic residual, not verified launderingTracked attacker holdings~$3.0BThird-party snapshot, Nov. 3, 09:10 UTC That distinction changes how I think about market impact. Bitcoin has no central token issuer that can blacklist a native coin. USDT and USDC do have issuers able to restrict token transfers at specific addresses. The stolen asset’s technical liquidity, its legal transferability and its practical ability to reach a market are three different questions. Sources: Binance incident statement; TRM Labs forensic reconstruction; Bitquery tracing. These sources have different observation cutoffs and should not be treated as a single reconciled ledger. A second theft exposes the danger of naming a victim too early The separate attack attributed in public reporting to Crédit Mutuel Arkéa offers a smaller but instructive version of the same problem. Investigator ZachXBT alleged withdrawals exceeding $133 million. The institution subsequently acknowledged an attack and fraudulent transactions to CoinDesk, but did not publicly validate the full amount or assign ownership of every wallet in the proposed transaction chain. A separate Bitquery investigation traced approximately $108.80 million in Ethereum USDC withdrawals from exchange accounts, using a November 2, 13:47 UTC cutoff. The difference from the $133 million allegation is at least $24.20 million. That is a reconciliation gap, not evidence that the larger allegation is false. It may reflect additional accounts, chains or activity outside the observed sample; none should be assumed without transactions and account ownership records. The cases should not be merged merely because they happened in the same news cycle. The Binance case has a separate North Korean attribution by U.S. authorities; the Arkéa-related investigation does not establish a shared attacker or common funds. FBI alert; Bitquery Ethereum analysis. The DeFi rebound looks better at one day than at one month The same tendency to compress distinct observations into a single headline appears in DeFi. CoinDesk described a strong one-session gain in its seven-member DeFi Select Index, with Injective and Ethena among the names discussed. That is a valid observation about a defined index over a defined interval. It does not demonstrate a broad, durable sector rotation. A wider fifteen-token DeFi-category basket, ranked by circulating market capitalization and excluding stablecoins, staked/wrapped representations and tokenized fund shares, showed an equal-weighted 24-hour mean return of about +2.05% at 13:53:48 UTC on November 4. From exchange thefts and frozen stablecoins to election-driven legislation and a sanctioned Moscow trading venue, the same question keeps resurfacing: who can actually move the money?
November 4, 2026 · Historical research snapshot
Editorial illustration; not a depiction of actual market data or an identified incident.

The most revealing number in crypto this week is not a token price. It is the gap between an asset that exists on a ledger and an asset that can actually be moved, redeemed or recovered. That gap runs through the reported Binance theft, a separate European financial-institution attack, an uneven DeFi rebound, and Moscow Exchange’s proposed crypto market. It also helps explain why election headlines and ETF flows should not be mistaken for settled outcomes.

My reading of the available evidence is that crypto’s most important November story is a contest over control. Blockchains can make transfers visible, but they cannot by themselves establish who owns an exchange account, compel a custodian to release funds, guarantee stablecoin redemption or turn a legislative proposal into law. The practical market sits between the ledger and the institutions that make it usable.

Binance reported approximately $6.34 billion in assets impacted by an October 29, 2026 attack, describing roughly $2.85 billion as frozen or intercepted in its November 3 account. Subtracting those figures produces about $3.49 billion not confirmed secured. That residual is not an audited measure of proceeds successfully cashed out, and it is not necessarily a current-price valuation of attacker holdings.

Separate tracing described large balances remaining identifiable in attacker-controlled wallets. A reported Bitquery snapshot at 09:10 UTC on November 3 valued tracked holdings at about $3 billion. That observation supports the possibility of future sell pressure, but a wallet balance is not a sell order. It is equally important that an issuer freeze is not the same as a legal recovery, and a customer reimbursement is not proof the original tokens have been returned.
Different measures of the Binance incident; figures are approximate and not additive.

That distinction changes how I think about market impact. Bitcoin has no central token issuer that can blacklist a native coin. USDT and USDC do have issuers able to restrict token transfers at specific addresses. The stolen asset’s technical liquidity, its legal transferability and its practical ability to reach a market are three different questions.

The same tendency to compress distinct observations into a single headline appears in DeFi. CoinDesk described a strong one-session gain in its seven-member DeFi Select Index, with Injective and Ethena among the names discussed. That is a valid observation about a defined index over a defined interval. It does not demonstrate a broad, durable sector rotation.

The basket’s thirty-day mean was about −21.33%, compared with Bitcoin’s −9.25%.

But reported float, recipient behavior and buy-side depth determine whether the supply ever reaches the market.Research window: November 3, 2026 – February 1, 2027 · Pricing and volume snapshot: November 3, 2026Illustration. Imagery is conceptual, not a representation of market transactions or verified token balances. A token unlock is often described as if a locked door opens and every token behind it instantly appears on an exchange. That is a useful image for a headline, but a poor model of market impact. A large tranche can overwhelm thin trading interest—or barely register if recipients do not sell. The question is not simply what unlocks. It is what becomes transferable, who controls it, and how much genuine demand is waiting.The 90 days from November 3, 2026 to February 1, 2027 contain several unusually large reported supply events. Monad and Ondo dominate different parts of the screen: one by the ratio of projected releases to circulating supply, the other by total dollar notional. A separate cluster—Falcon Finance, MemeCore and Cronos—looks especially consequential after comparing prospective release value with reported daily trading volume.My interpretation is that the headline unlock league table obscures two very different kinds of risk. Dilution describes how much the visible supply base might expand. Liquidity describes the ability of buyers to absorb possible transfers without moving price. A token can score modestly on the first dimension and look alarming on the second.A scheduled unlock is a supply event, not proof of a sell order. Float, recipient incentives and real order-book depth determine its market significance. The same market snapshot reports about $6.92 million in daily trading volume. The quotient—40.3 times volume—is remarkable as an indicator of potential liquidity mismatch.But even the numerator is disputed. It is the larger nominal-dollar story, yet its eventual price effect may be driven less by the headline number than by whether foundation, investor or ecosystem recipients immediately acquire transferable inventory.Neither ratio predicts a specific decline. Nor does a release of previously locked assets necessarily dilute the economic rights of existing holders in the same way that newly minted tokens would. Reported turnover in the same snapshot was only about $1.47 million per day. That makes the theoretical release roughly 12 times daily activity. Its prospective 1.17 billion CRO strategic-reserve allocation is only about 2.3% of reported circulation, but its value is nearly 20 times one day's reported trading. Its intended distribution and wallet behavior matter more than the size of the reserve label.Meanwhile, LayerZero and Plasma show high calculated float additions but lower gross unlock-to-volume ratios in the same snapshot. Founders, long-duration investors and protocol treasuries face different incentives. Second, recipients may hedge in advance, shifting the price response before the official date. Later-month percentages should not be extrapolated using a fixed November 3 supply denominator. The uncomfortable part: the data has a float problemThe most tempting rankings use unlock tokens divided by circulating supply and unlock dollar value divided by daily volume. Both can be calculated. Neither alone measures the variable a trader actually needs: newly transferable supply that is likely to seek buyers. Reported circulation can include inactive or effectively constrained inventory. Trading volume describes turnover, not the cumulative limit orders available at a given price.There are also irreducible schedule disagreements. MON estimates range from 15.6 billion to 17.11 billion tokens. Ondo's date is reported as January 17 or 18. LayerZero dates differ by a day in some calendars. Starknet figures range from approximately 127 million to 226 million. PUMP's reported monthly release sizes are inconsistent enough that I would not collapse them into one confident figure. Any model treating those competing inputs as a single known truth is overstating its quality.For a more useful pressure estimate, I would multiply the unlock notional by an evidence-based estimate of the immediately sellable share, then compare that amount with genuine spot demand: verified buy-side depth, replenishment rates and recent execution volume after excluding suspicious turnover. The result would be conditional rather than predictive, but it would be much closer to the question that actually matters.What would prove this thesis wrong?The high-pressure case would weaken if the relevant tokens remain contractually restricted, identified recipient wallets do not send supply toward markets, or genuine spot bids replenish sufficiently to absorb transfers. It would also weaken if exchanges already priced the event well in advance. Conversely, rising recipient-linked deposits combined with falling bid depth, aggressive spot selling and failed price recoveries would strengthen the case for near-term market stress.Even then, an unlock is not a standalone trading strategy. For a short-horizon position, price structure, funding, open interest, spot cumulative volume delta and a defensible stop are necessary before evaluating reward against risk. Without those confirmations, the analytical decision is to monitor rather than manufacture a trade.What I would watch firstMonad is the highest-priority schedule reconciliation and exchange-flow investigation. Ondo is the largest nominal release and deserves focused analysis as January approaches. Falcon Finance, MemeCore and Cronos merit attention because the notional size of their candidate releases is disproportionate to current reported turnover. GRVT and WET need credible liquidity and transferable-float measurements before they can be responsibly ranked with the others.The more important conclusion is structural. Crypto market dashboards make circulating supply look like a single objective number, while actual access to supply is mediated by contracts, institutions, trading venues and incentives. A token unlock reveals where that abstraction may fail. The calendar is the beginning of the investigation, not its answer.My bottom line: The next 90 days contain significant prospective supply changes, but a calendar cannot establish an impending sell-off. What matters is the gap between tokens that may become transferable and demand that is genuinely willing to meet them. Until that gap is measured, the appropriate classification is a research watchlist—not a directional trade signal. A strategic-reserve release should not be treated as automatic selling. Its intended distribution and wallet behavior matter more than the size of the reserve label.

Meanwhile, LayerZero and Plasma show high calculated float additions but lower gross unlock-to-volume ratios in the same snapshot. That does not make them safe: gross volume can be inflated, liquidity fragments across exchanges and tokens may trade in thin conditions even when daily volume appears healthy. It does argue against assigning the same supply-risk label to every large circulating-supply change.

First, the new recipients may hold. Founders, long-duration investors and protocol treasuries face different incentives. Second, recipients may hedge in advance, shifting the price response before the official date. Third, legitimate market makers or existing buy interest may absorb release-related transfers without a sustained decline. Conversely, selling can arrive before the unlock if holders reposition in anticipation, and an adverse macro event can overwhelm any token-specific effect.

That makes recipient wallets, transfer restrictions, on-chain exchange deposits, spot taker activity and actual order-book resilience the decisive next tests. An exchange-inflow increase is stronger evidence of possible distribution than a calendar cell, but it is still not proof of a completed sale.

Selected material calendar entries, grouped by month. Where providers disagree, the conflicting quantity or date is intentionally shown. A recurring vesting tranche is not necessarily equivalent to a one-time cliff.
This is a material-event selection, not a complete ledger of all linear vesting emissions. Later-month percentages should not be extrapolated using a fixed November 3 supply denominator.

The most tempting rankings use unlock tokens divided by circulating supply and unlock dollar value divided by daily volume. Both can be calculated. Neither alone measures the variable a trader actually needs: newly transferable supply that is likely to seek buyers. Reported circulation can include inactive or effectively constrained inventory. Trading volume describes turnover, not the cumulative limit orders available at a given price.

There are also irreducible schedule disagreements. MON estimates range from 15.6 billion to 17.11 billion tokens. Ondo's date is reported as January 17 or 18. LayerZero dates differ by a day in some calendars. Starknet figures range from approximately 127 million to 226 million. PUMP's reported monthly release sizes are inconsistent enough that I would not collapse them into one confident figure. Any model treating those competing inputs as a single known truth is overstating its quality.

For a more useful pressure estimate, I would multiply the unlock notional by an evidence-based estimate of the immediately sellable share, then compare that amount with genuine spot demand: verified buy-side depth, replenishment rates and recent execution volume after excluding suspicious turnover. The result would be conditional rather than predictive, but it would be much closer to the question that actually matters.

The high-pressure case would weaken if the relevant tokens remain contractually restricted, identified recipient wallets do not send supply toward markets, or genuine spot bids replenish sufficiently to absorb transfers. It would also weaken if exchanges already priced the event well in advance. Conversely, rising recipient-linked deposits combined with falling bid depth, aggressive spot selling and failed price recoveries would strengthen the case for near-term market stress.

Even then, an unlock is not a standalone trading strategy. For a short-horizon position, price structure, funding, open interest, spot cumulative volume delta and a defensible stop are necessary before evaluating reward against risk. Without those confirmations, the analytical decision is to monitor rather than manufacture a trade.

Monad is the highest-priority schedule reconciliation and exchange-flow investigation. Ondo is the largest nominal release and deserves focused analysis as January approaches. Falcon Finance, MemeCore and Cronos merit attention because the notional size of their candidate releases is disproportionate to current reported turnover. GRVT and WET need credible liquidity and transferable-float measurements before they can be responsibly ranked with the others.

The more important conclusion is structural. Crypto market dashboards make circulating supply look like a single objective number, while actual access to supply is mediated by contracts, institutions, trading venues and incentives. A token unlock reveals where that abstraction may fail. The calendar is the beginning of the investigation, not its answer.

My bottom line: The next 90 days contain significant prospective supply changes, but a calendar cannot establish an impending sell-off. What matters is the gap between tokens that may become transferable and demand that is genuinely willing to meet them. Until that gap is measured, the appropriate classification is a research watchlist—not a directional trade signal.

Sources and methodology: Published schedule comparisons: DefiLlama calendar, Toolz unlocks, TokenToria and MrNasDog. Market-price, market-cap, circulation and 24-hour volume references: CoinPaprika snapshot, November 3, 2026, approximately 20:27 UTC. These third-party schedule sources were summarized in the underlying November 3 research; original vesting contracts were not comprehensively audited.

Scope: All valuations are historical snapshot estimates, not live quotes. Unlock dates, sizes and supply classifications may change. Token prices, volume, holder intent and actual liquidity are not forecast. Some values are contradictory or incomplete and are labeled accordingly. This publication provides market research, not financial advice.

deepbook-supply-transparency.text: Independent Market NotesTokenomics / Investigative analysisDeepBook’s Supply Question: Is the Treasury Locked or Discretionary?A reported 5.27-billion-token holder, conflicting circulation figures, and an unanswered question about who can move DEEP.Research snapshot: November 3, 2026 · Historical figures, not live quotes Editorial illustration. The lock is conceptual, not a depiction of a verified on-chain vault. A token can have a functioning product, measurable trading activity and a plausible economic role—and still leave investors unable to answer a basic question: how much supply is actually available to move? That is the tension at the center of DeepBook, the Sui-based on-chain order-book infrastructure project. Public token-holder pages identify one address as holding roughly 5.27 billion DEEP, more than half of the token’s stated 10-billion maximum. Yet two major market-data providers have published sharply different circulating-supply figures. And the project's allocation disclosures describe a large ecosystem treasury without conclusively identifying the controls on the reported holder. What interests me is not the size of that balance in isolation. Large protocol treasuries are common. The consequential question is whether the tokens are subject to enforceable release restrictions or held under administrative discretion. Those are different economic risks, even when both arrangements are described as a long-term ecosystem allocation. A real protocol, and a separate supply problem DeepBook is not merely a token searching for a purpose. It provides shared on-chain central-limit-order-book infrastructure for applications on Sui. The DEEP token can be used to pay trading fees and obtain staking-related benefits. Official documentation also allows certain fees to be paid in input tokens, meaning DEEP is useful without being mandatory in every transaction. Sui’s DeepBook documentation describes the protocol and its operating model. Protocol activity gives the project an empirical foundation. In snapshots discussed during this investigation, DefiLlama reported roughly $178 million–$211 million in trailing 30-day DEX volume, with tokenholder-revenue estimates around $8,859–$10,981. These are different observations at different retrieval times, not a single synchronized dataset; their methodology and the relationship between reported revenue and economic benefits to holders require scrutiny. The underlying DefiLlama protocol page is the appropriate reference for updated values. Those numbers matter because they establish a reason to investigate DEEP seriously. They do not resolve the supply denominator used to value the token. Two circulating supplies for the same token On November 3, 2026, CoinGecko’s supply breakdown reported 2.5 billion DEEP circulating, alongside approximately 6.259 billion outstanding and 10 billion total. CoinMarketCap’s quote data reported approximately 6.014 billion circulating and 10 billion total. The CoinMarketCap figure was also labeled as self-reported circulating supply. Provider snapshots, November 3, 2026, approximately 13:24–13:26 UTC. Figures rounded.MeasureCoinGeckoCoinMarketCapCirculating DEEP2.500B6.014BMaximum / total supply10.000B10.000BReported market capitalization~$37.9M~$93.9MFully diluted valuation~$151.6M~$156.1MProvenance limitationNo noncirculating wallets identified in supply-breakdown responseCirculating supply also designated self-reported Both estimates placed DEEP within the $1 million–$100 million small-cap research range at those timestamps. But they describe very different floats. Using the two circulating-supply figures produces a roughly 2.4-fold difference in implied capitalization at a common token price. The modest difference in the providers’ fully diluted valuations reflects differing price snapshots, not a different maximum supply. How much of the maximum supply is counted as circulating?CoinGecko25.00%CoinMarketCap60.14%Scale begins at zero and ends at 100% of the 10B maximum. Historical provider estimates, not independently reconciled on-chain circulation. There are legitimate reasons for data services to disagree. One may exclude ecosystem-controlled balances that another counts as transferable. One may rely on a project-supplied figure while another applies its own classification. The discrepancy is therefore evidence of a measurement problem, not evidence by itself of concealment or misconduct. The address that changes the question GeckoTerminal’s holder information identifies the following Sui address as the largest reported DEEP holder: 0x9548232f9cebbc1eec56cfb25b99f61e17924b4908248c260c8d70100c59c70d Its reported balance is approximately 5.27 billion DEEP, or 52.7% of maximum supply. A separate holder-distribution page showed a similarly sized top balance and a second address holding roughly 1.62 billion DEEP. The two reported positions together account for approximately 69% of maximum supply. These are address-level concentrations, not proof that two people or entities beneficially own the tokens. See GeckoTerminal’s DEEP/SUI pool and holder information. A key distinction follows: a blockchain address can belong to a treasury, custodian, vesting system, exchange or individual. A balance alone does not reveal who can authorize transfers or what restrictions apply. What the treasury disclosures actually say DeepBook’s published tokenomics assign 61.57% of total supply—6.157 billion DEEP—to ecosystem growth. The allocation is close enough in scale to the reported 5.27-billion holder to make a treasury connection plausible. It does not prove that connection. A Sui-hosted DeepBook whitepaper describes the token’s design and allocation, while the project’s token page describes ecosystem distribution. A separate Kraken-published DEEP disclosure describes the Sui Foundation as the initial holder of a large ecosystem allocation and refers to an on-chain ecosystem vault with a multiyear release program. The documents do not, in the evidence available here, authenticate the reported largest-holder address as that vault. There is also a subtle but crucial ambiguity in the language of release. A project can say tokens were “unlocked” at token generation while planning to distribute them over seven years. That may mean the tokens were technically transferable but administratively reserved. Alternatively, tokens could be held inside a Move object with time-based withdrawal restrictions. Both arrangements can support a multiyear distribution plan; only one necessarily makes that plan enforceable by code. The missing fact is not the intended schedule. It is the authority to override it. Without the vault object, controlling Move module, ownership configuration and withdrawal history, a published distribution plan cannot establish that transfers are technically prohibited. Three explanations remain viable 1. A genuinely restricted ecosystem vault The large address could correspond to an ecosystem-controlled object with enforceable vesting or timelock conditions. Under this interpretation, at least some treasury balances may be properly excluded from circulating supply until release. Confirmation would require identifying the relevant Sui object and demonstrating the actual withdrawal rules, including any privileged bypass. 2. A treasury governed by authorized signers The tokens could instead sit in ordinary transferable coin objects controlled by an authorized address or multisignature arrangement. A seven-year release plan could still be sincere and consistently followed, but the restriction would be institutional rather than automatically enforced. The economic distinction is that authorized parties may have greater discretion to accelerate transfers. 3. An address unrelated to the Foundation treasury The holder could represent another custody or protocol arrangement. Matching its balance to the original ecosystem allocation is suggestive, not identifying evidence. A reliable attribution would require an official address statement, an unambiguous creation or funding trail, or both. None of these explanations has been conclusively established. It would be premature to call the balance either a verified locked vault or an unrestricted Foundation wallet. Why vesting trackers do not settle it Third-party token-unlock dashboards have shown different unlocked-supply estimates and classifications for DEEP. Some distinguish scheduled vesting from circulation; others apply allocation-specific assumptions. These datasets can be useful leads, but they cannot replace inspection of the relevant Sui objects and transaction history. One more complication is the token’s architecture. The official Sui documentation identifies the native coin type as 0xdeeb7a4662eec9f2f3def03fb937a663dddaa2e215b8078a284d026b7946c270::deep::DEEP. DeepBook’s core contracts are upgradeable, but upgradeability of the trading protocol does not by itself establish the transfer controls on a separate ecosystem treasury. The relevant treasury implementation must be examined on its own terms. See Sui’s contract information. Why the difference matters for valuation When circulating supply is uncertain, market capitalization becomes a conditional estimate. A lower denominator can make a token appear smaller relative to its activity, revenue or peers. A larger denominator can make the same price look considerably more expensive. Neither interpretation should be adopted without understanding what the excluded tokens are and who can move them. The distinction also changes how investors should think about dilution. A time-locked allocation introduces scheduled future supply. A discretionary treasury introduces governance, custody and disclosure risk. Both can be managed responsibly; they simply require different evidence. Trading liquidity adds another layer. A few observed automated-market-maker pools showed relatively modest reserves, but those snapshots did not capture DeepBook’s own order books or all centralized venues. It would be misleading to treat that narrow sample as the token’s total executable liquidity. The protocol’s documented DEEP/SUI and DEEP/USDC order-book pools warrant separate depth analysis. What would settle the question For a definitive answer, I would want four pieces of public evidence: an authoritative attribution of the largest-holder address; the relevant treasury object ID and Move type; the code and capabilities governing withdrawal, upgrade and administrator access; and a historical reconciliation of deposits, releases and remaining balances against the published allocation schedule. Those facts could validate the restricted-vault interpretation. They could instead show a discretionary treasury following a voluntary distribution policy. Or they could reveal that the reported address is unrelated to the Foundation allocation. Any of those outcomes would be more informative than repeating a circulating-supply number without examining its assumptions. The real test is verifiability My conclusion is deliberately narrower than an accusation: DeepBook has demonstrable utility, but the public evidence considered here does not establish how the largest reported DEEP balance is controlled. Nor does it reconcile the competing circulating-supply estimates. For a protocol built on transparent, programmable finance, that gap is worth closing. The strongest disclosure would not be another promise about long-term alignment. It would be a verifiable address, a verifiable contract and a clear explanation of which tokens can actually move. Until then, the honest description is not “locked” or “unlocked.” It is unresolved. ◆ Sources and methodology notesDeepBook: DEEP token and distribution — project allocation and release language.Sui: DeepBook token whitepaper — original design and allocation framework; note that historical allocation percentages may differ from later documents.Sui: DeepBook V3 contract information — canonical DEEP type, protocol versions and order-book identifiers.CoinGecko: DeepBook and CoinMarketCap: DeepBook Protocol — differing November 3, 2026 supply and valuation snapshots.GeckoTerminal: DEEP/SUI pool — reported largest-holder address and balance.DefiLlama: DeepBook — protocol activity and revenue categories; figures are time-dependent.DefiLlama: DeepBook unlocks and DropsTab: DEEP vesting — competing unlock methodologies, not definitive proof of wallet-level restrictions.All market and holder figures are historical observations discussed as of November 3, 2026. Reported balances, labels and supply classifications are not presented as a complete independent on-chain audit. No allegation of misconduct follows from the unresolved custody question.
